nameStory: MacGregor's wildrye honors an early botanist who helped identify and describe this grass species. The 'wildrye' part of the name refers to its relationship to cultivated rye, though this wild cousin grows freely in nature rather than in farmers' fields.
description: MacGregor's wildrye is a native bunch grass that forms clumps rather than spreading by runners like some of its relatives. This medium-height grass typically reaches 2-4 feet tall, with narrow green leaves and distinctive seed heads that appear in late summer. It's one of our less common wild ryes, preferring specific habitats and sometimes hybridizing with its more common cousins.

idTips.label: Seed Heads
idTips.description: Dense, narrow spike-like seed heads that feel slightly rough to the touch, with individual seeds arranged closely along the central stem rather than in loose, drooping clusters

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Flat, narrow grass blades that feel smooth on top but may be slightly rough along the edges when you run your finger along them

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms distinct clumps or bunches rather than creating a spreading mat, with multiple stems arising from the same base

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Upright, unbranched stems that feel firm and solid when gently squeezed, typically smooth to the touch

habitat: MacGregor's wildrye grows in prairies, open woodlands, and woodland edges, often in areas with rich, well-drained soils. In New England, look for it in natural openings, along forest borders, or in restored grassland areas where native plant communities are being encouraged.

seasonality.spring: New green shoots emerge from the base, forming fresh clumps of narrow leaves that grow steadily taller.
seasonality.summer: The grass reaches full height and develops its characteristic seed heads in late summer, which start green and gradually mature.
seasonality.fall: Seed heads turn golden-brown and release their seeds, while the foliage begins to fade from green to tan.
seasonality.winter: Dried stems and seed heads may persist, appearing as tan or brown clumps that rustle softly in winter winds.

funFact: MacGregor's wildrye is such a genetic mixer that it readily creates hybrid offspring with its relatives Virginia wildrye and bottlebrush grass, sometimes making identification a puzzle even for botanists since the hybrid children can look like combinations of their parents!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with Virginia wildrye and Canada wild rye, but MacGregor's wildrye typically has denser, more compact seed heads. Memory trick: MacGregor likes to keep things 'compact' - his seed heads are tighter and more crowded together than his looser relatives.
contextualKnowledge: With only one recorded observation in New England, this grass is extremely rare in our region and represents the northeastern edge of its range. Finding one would be a significant botanical discovery worth reporting to local naturalist groups.
compareHints: Among the wild ryes, MacGregor's has more compact seed heads than the droopy, loose spikes of bottlebrush grass and lacks the distinctive 'bottle brush' appearance of that species. Compared to Virginia wildrye, its seed heads are denser and more tightly packed, while Canada wild rye tends to have more nodding or curved seed heads rather than the upright spikes typical of MacGregor's.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its wild rye relatives, bottlebrush grass is the clear standout with its extremely long bristles - other Elymus species like Virginia wild rye or Canada wild rye have much shorter bristles or awns that don't create that distinctive brush appearance.
Unlike its native relatives like Virginia wildrye and Canada wild rye, quack grass spreads aggressively by rhizomes rather than just growing in clumps.
Virginia wildrye is the most delicate-looking of our wild ryes, with shorter awns and a more compact seed head than Canada wild rye.

Among the wild ryes in New England, Canada wild rye stands out for its distinctly nodding seed heads - Virginia wildrye holds its seed heads more upright, while bottlebrush grass has much more prominent, messy-looking bristles.

Among New England's wild ryes, river wild rye stands out for its preference for wet areas and its notably long awns - up to an inch compared to the shorter bristles of Virginia wildrye or Canada wild rye.
Compared to its wild rye cousins, Wiegand's is notably more compact and clump-forming than the spreading Canada wild rye or the taller, more robust Virginia wild rye.
Among New England's wild ryes, slender wheatgrass stands out for having the narrowest, most compressed flower spike pressed tightly to the stem.

Among its Elymus relatives, silky wild rye stands out for its soft, hairy texture - bottlebrush grass has distinctive spreading seed heads, Canada wild rye is much taller and coarser, and Virginia wildrye lacks the silky hairs.
